name: RU58841

lead: RU58841 is a non-steroidal topical antiandrogen originally developed by Roussel Uclaf and later investigated for acne, pattern hair loss and excess hair growth. Hair-loss communities use it hoping to protect scalp hair without the side effects of oral DHT blockers.

It binds the androgen receptor and blocks DHT from activating it in scalp follicles, intended to act locally. The published research is cell, rodent, macaque and xenograft work from the 1990s, including the stumptail macaque; no controlled human trial on hair is known. Success reports come mainly from forum posts.

paras: Users apply it to the scalp as a solution, typically daily, as an alternative or add-on to finasteride or dutasteride. It is sold as a research chemical, often in alcohol-based liquids.
Human toxicity, systemic absorption and long-term effects are not established. It was never approved, and vendor products vary in purity. Alcohol-based solutions can irritate the scalp.

angle.text: RU58841 is a topical antiandrogen used by people hoping to treat hair loss without oral drug side effects. It blocks the androgen receptor in the scalp follicle, aiming to reduce miniaturisation and keep hair. Published work is animal and cell research, and success reports come mainly from forums.

lead: RU58841, also known as PSK-3841 or HMR-3841, is a nonsteroidal antiandrogen originally developed by the French company Roussel Uclaf. It was later investigated by ProStrakan (earlier ProSkelia and Strakan) as a topical treatment for androgen-dependent conditions including acne, pattern hair loss and excess hair growth [1]. It is structurally related to nilutamide and other nonsteroidal antiandrogens [1][2].

In hair-loss communities it is discussed as a topical androgen-receptor blocker: rather than lowering dihydrotestosterone (DHT) the way finasteride and dutasteride do, it is meant to sit on the receptor in scalp follicles and keep DHT from acting there, so that follicles keep their size and hair stays thicker and denser [3][4][5]. People who use it for appearance describe it as a way to hold on to or regain scalp hair, and some hope it can improve oily, acne-prone skin by acting on sebaceous glands [6][7].

It has never been approved as a medicine. Published research consists of cell, rodent, macaque and xenograft studies from the 1990s, and no controlled human trial of its effect on hair is known [6][8][9][10]. Its development was discontinued, and Wikipedia lists it among nonsteroidal antiandrogens developed for topical acne or hair loss that were abandoned [1][2]. Users in hair-loss and bodybuilding forums nonetheless obtain it as a chemical sold outside regulated pharmacy channels and use it alone or alongside finasteride, dutasteride or minoxidil [11][12][13][14][15][16].
infobox: Androgen receptor antagonist; does not lower androgen levels [3][2]

paras: RU58841 was explored for androgen-dependent skin and hair conditions: androgenetic alopecia, acne and hirsutism [1]. In pattern hair loss, scalp follicles are genetically sensitive to androgens and dihydrotestosterone is the main androgen acting at the dermal papilla, which is why drugs that block it, whether by inhibiting 5-alpha-reductase or by occupying the receptor, are the main medical approach [5]. Patent filings from 2000 and 2001 list RU58841 among antiandrogens that could be combined with relaxin in hair-growth compositions [17][18][19].

On looksmax.org and T Nation, users describe it as an experimental hair-loss treatment, usually discussed alongside minoxidil and 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors [11][13][14][20][16][21]. Threads ask whether it can be run without a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor, why anyone would still use finasteride alongside it, and whether it can be mixed with minoxidil [15][22][16]. A looksmax.org member has also asked whether blocking androgens locally could reduce sebum, pore size and acne on the face, as an alternative to isotretinoin; the thread presents this as a theory [7].
No studies found in humans for hair loss. The existing research is preclinical and is summarised below as such.

In a 1997 controlled study from De Brouwer, Van Neste and colleagues, twenty productive scalp grafts from balding men were kept on nude mice conditioned with testosterone and treated five days a week with blinded solutions of 1% RU58841 in ethanol or ethanol alone for six months; the abstract reports that control grafts had 28 active follicles, of which only two (7 percent) began a second hair cycle, while treated grafts bore 29 active follicles [10]. A 1998 study led by Chawnshang Chang's group found that topical RU58841 increased hair density, thickness and length in the stumptailed macaque model of androgenetic alopecia, with no systemic effects detected, and that in prostate cell assays its potency as an androgen-receptor antagonist was comparable to hydroxyflutamide [8]. A 1999 co-culture study used RU58841 to abolish testosterone-induced inhibition of keratinocyte growth in macaque dermal papilla cells and identified supervillin as a testosterone-downregulated gene [9].

In the fuzzy rat, a model for acne, 1% topical RU58841 applied for two months produced sebaceous gland regression equivalent to castration, greater than finasteride [6]. A 1998 prostate cell-line study reported that, in cells overexpressing the AR coactivator ARA70, several antiandrogens including RU58841 could act as agonists, a finding the authors used to motivate better antiandrogen design [23].

RU58841 blocks the androgen receptor rather than lowering androgen production, a distinction forum users draw when comparing it with 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors [3][24][2]. Nonsteroidal antiandrogens in general act as competitive receptor antagonists that stop testosterone and DHT from activating the receptor [2]. In animals RU58841 is metabolised to cyanonilutamide (RU-56279), which has low receptor affinity but notable antiandrogenic activity, and to RU-59416, which has very low affinity [1]. Wikipedia attributes the description of these metabolites to a 1994 rat study [1].
The macaque study authors noted that the compound might cause systemic effects after topical use but reported none in that model [8]. No published human pharmacokinetic data are known.

Chemically it is a hydantoin-based molecule, 4-[3-(4-hydroxybutyl)-4,4-dimethyl-2,5-dioxo-1-imidazolidinyl]-2-(trifluoromethyl)benzonitrile, with formula C17H18F3N3O3. It is structurally similar to RU-58642 but has a different side chain [1]. A 2026 organic chemistry paper used RU58841 as an example of a bioactive alcohol in a synthetic-method study unrelated to hair [25].

No human safety profile has been published. Animal and cell studies have examined efficacy rather than toxicity in people, and the 1998 authors flagged the theoretical possibility of systemic exposure after topical application [8]. Wikipedia notes that other nonsteroidal antiandrogens are associated with effects such as liver toxicity (flutamide), lung effects (nilutamide) and seizure risk (enzalutamide), though these are oral drugs for prostate cancer rather than topical products [2].

Forum members describe use alongside testosterone replacement or anabolic steroids to manage hair loss [13][26][27]. One looksmax.org member wrote that after months of use he had noticed loss of strength and muscle gain and a lump he identified as gynecomastia, and that libido increased after a week off; another member replied that antiandrogens might be expected to have side effects, while others said related topical antiandrogens such as fluridil and pyrilutamide are not reported to do so [28]. These are individual anecdotes, not trial data.

sections.h: Related compounds and the topical antiandrogen field
paras: RU58841 sits in a small group of topical antiandrogens. Wikipedia lists cioteronel, inocoterone acetate and RU-58841 as nonsteroidal antiandrogens developed for acne or hair loss and discontinued, either for insufficient effectiveness or during phase I trials [2]. Topilutamide (fluridil) was introduced in 2003, is marketed as a topical hair-loss product in the Czech Republic and Slovakia and has not been approved by the FDA or EMA for androgenetic alopecia [29].

Clascoterone (Winlevi), a topical androgen receptor antagonist from Cassiopea, was approved by the US FDA for acne in August 2020; two phase 3 trials for scalp hair loss were disclosed in December 2025 and both reported significant improvement in hair counts versus placebo, per Wikipedia [30]. Pyrilutamide (KX-826) from Suzhou Kintor Pharmaceuticals was in phase 3 trials for pattern hair loss as of February 2025 [31]. On looksmax.org, a thread title reports that a prominent poster now recommends pyrilutamide over RU58841, showing how some members treat the newer compounds as successors [32].

Finasteride, approved for male pattern hair loss in 1997, lowers DHT by inhibiting type II and III 5-alpha-reductase. Wikipedia notes that sexual side effects can persist after stopping in some users, that a proposed post-finasteride syndrome is disputed, and that the European Medicines Agency confirmed in 2025 that suicidal thoughts can occur as a side effect of finasteride and dutasteride [4]. Forum users often cite these concerns when explaining interest in a topical blocker [3][24].

Roussel Uclaf developed the compound, and per Wikipedia it was initially developed in the 1980s [1]. A 1994 paper by Battmann and colleagues described it as a new specific topical antiandrogen and a candidate for acne, androgenetic alopecia and hirsutism, and a 2005 study by Münster and colleagues described an RU 58841 myristate ester prodrug for topical use [1]. Animal hair studies were published in 1997 to 1999 [8][9][10]. The company ProStrakan later investigated it before it was dropped [1][2].

A T Nation poster in 2013 described it as abandoned partway through trials; this is a forum characterisation [33]. A T Nation thread in 2013 described it as an extremely powerful topical antiandrogen that is not a commercially available product [27]. In 2004 a poster asked whether others had heard of it [34].

RU58841 is not a marketed drug in any jurisdiction covered by the sources [2]. It circulates as a research chemical in hair-loss and bodybuilding forums. T Nation users mention that the compound is costly, that some consider the raw powder to save money, and that a vehicle that lets the topical work must be found [11][33]. Looksmax.org has threads on where to get it, how long a vial lasts, and how to combine it with microneedling or minoxidil; this article does not reproduce preparation or sourcing details [16][35].

The topic belongs to the wider hair-loss and hardmaxxing discussion in looksmaxxing culture, where Wikipedia notes that off-label substances are among the interventions in the practice [36]. A teenage looksmax.org member describes planning to pair it with oral minoxidil on top of ketoconazole shampoo, with dutasteride considered after finishing development [20].. Hair-loss forum members describe it as an option for people on testosterone therapy or steroids who want to keep hair [13][14][26].

No regulator has approved RU58841 for any use, and it is not covered by a marketing authorisation in the United States or Europe [2]. Products sold online fall outside pharmaceutical regulation, and a T Nation poster notes that finding a vehicle that lets the topical work is part of using it [33].

lore.intro: On T Nation, looksmax.org and similar forums, RU58841 appears as an option for people managing hair loss on testosterone therapy or steroids, or who want to avoid oral finasteride [13][14][26][15].

timeline.event: Roussel Uclaf develops RU58841 as a nonsteroidal antiandrogen [1].
Battmann and colleagues describe it as a new specific topical antiandrogen; a rat study describes its metabolites [1].
Study of RU58841 on human balding scalp grafts in nude mice published; fuzzy rat sebaceous gland study also published [6][10].
Macaque study reports increased hair density and length with topical application; ARA70 cell study reports agonist behaviour of several antiandrogens in coactivator-rich cells [8][23].
A US patent lists RU58841 among antiandrogens that could be combined with relaxin for hair growth [17].
Münster and colleagues describe a myristate ester prodrug for topical use [1].
T Nation threads describe it as an abandoned topical antiandrogen used by some hair-loss forum members [33][27].
Topical antiandrogen clascoterone is approved by the FDA for acne [30].
Pyrilutamide is in phase 3 trials for hair loss and clascoterone scalp hair-loss trials report results [31][30].
